subChunks.title: Flame Graphs, Heap Dumps & Thread Dump Analysis
subChunks.hookHtml: A profiler is the difference between an engineer who spends a week guessing and an engineer who finds the problem in an afternoon. Profiling is not a specialist skill — it is a core engineering tool that every senior developer must be able to reach for immediately when performance or stability issues arise.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Types of Profiling

  • CPU profiling: where is time spent? Produces a call tree or flame graph. Tools: async-profiler, JFR (Java Flight Recorder), VisualVM.
  • Memory profiling: where are allocations coming from? What is retained? Produces an allocation profile and heap dump. Tools: JFR, Eclipse Memory Analyser (MAT), VisualVM.
  • Thread profiling: are threads blocked? What are they waiting for? Produces a thread dump. Tools: jstack, VisualVM, JFR.

Flame Graphs

A flame graph is a visualisation of a CPU profile. Each horizontal bar is a stack frame; width represents the percentage of time the frame was on the CPU stack. The bottom is the entry point (main); the top shows what was running. Wide frames near the top of the flame are your hotspots.

# Capture a flame graph with async-profiler (attach to PID)
./profiler.sh -e cpu -d 30 -f flamegraph.html <pid>

# Or via Java agent at startup
-agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=flamegraph.html

Heap Dumps

A heap dump is a snapshot of all objects in heap memory at a point in time. Used to find: what objects are consuming the most memory, which objects are unexpectedly retained (leaks), the shortest path from GC root to a retained object.

# Capture heap dump with jcmd (attaches to running JVM)
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

# Or on OutOfMemoryError (add to JVM flags)
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/

# Analyse with Eclipse MAT: Leak Suspects Report highlights
# the biggest retained object trees automatically

Thread Dumps

A thread dump lists all JVM threads with their current state and stack trace. Use it to diagnose: deadlocks (threads waiting on each other's locks), thread pool exhaustion (all threads BLOCKED or WAITING), and stuck operations.

# Capture thread dump
jstack <pid> > threaddump.txt
# Or: kill -3 <pid>  (sends SIGQUIT, JVM prints to stdout)

# Key states in output:
# RUNNABLE   — actively running or runnable (may be in OS I/O wait)
# BLOCKED    — waiting to acquire a monitor lock
# WAITING    — waiting indefinitely (Object.wait(), LockSupport.park())
# TIMED_WAITING — sleeping or waiting with timeout
# DEADLOCK   — jstack explicitly labels deadlocked threads at the bottom

Java Flight Recorder (JFR)

Built into the JVM (Java 11+, free since Java 11). Low-overhead continuous recording — safe to run in production. Records CPU, allocations, GC events, I/O, exceptions, lock contention in a single .jfr file. Open with JDK Mission Control (JMC) for visual analysis.

# Start recording with jcmd
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile duration=60s filename=recording.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=profile

storyBeats.text: The Academy's tournament platform ground to a halt every night at midnight. Six engineers blamed it on the batch job, the network, the database, the cache. The seventh opened a flame graph. In ten minutes she showed everyone: one method, called 40 million times a night, was calling System.currentTimeMillis() to format log lines that nobody ever read.

storyBeats.speaker: Systems Investigator Dael
storyBeats.text: A flame graph shows you time as space. Wide bars are expensive. When you see a wide bar you didn't expect, that is your bottleneck. Everything else is noise. I have seen teams spend weeks on architectural 'fixes' that would never have helped because they never looked at the flame graph.

storyBeats.speaker: Systems Investigator Dael
storyBeats.text: Thread dumps diagnose a completely different category of problem: not slowness but stuckness. When your service stops responding — not slow, stopped — you need a thread dump. If all your threads are BLOCKED waiting for a lock, or WAITING on an empty queue, the thread dump tells you exactly which lock and what is holding it.

storyBeats.speaker: Thread dump deadlock signature
storyBeats.text:
# Thread dump shows:
"Thread-1" BLOCKED on lock 0x000abc (held by Thread-2)
"Thread-2" BLOCKED on lock 0x000def (held by Thread-1)

# JVM explicitly labels it:
Found one Java-level deadlock:
  Thread-1 waiting for Thread-2
  Thread-2 waiting for Thread-1

# Fix: always acquire locks in a consistent order across all threads

storyBeats.speaker: Systems Investigator Dael
storyBeats.text: Java Flight Recorder should be on in production — always. It costs under 1% overhead. When something goes wrong, you already have the data. An OOM in production at 3am with no JFR recording means a very long night of guessing. With JFR you look at the allocation profile from the minutes before the OOM and the answer is usually obvious.

learningObjectives: Describe the three types of profiling (CPU, memory, thread) and the question each answers
Read a flame graph and identify the hottest code path from visual width
Capture a thread dump and identify BLOCKED, WAITING, and deadlocked threads
Explain what Java Flight Recorder records and why it is safe to run in production
commonMistakes: Using System.out.println timing as a substitute for a profiler — misses the real hotspot
Running a profiler for too short a duration — GC events and rare code paths are missed
Ignoring thread state in thread dumps — confusing RUNNABLE with 'doing useful work' (it may be in I/O wait)
Analysing heap dumps without understanding GC roots — looking at total size instead of retained size misleads
assessmentCriteria: Can describe what a flame graph visualises and how to read it to find the CPU hotspot
Can name the JVM tools for capturing a heap dump, thread dump, and JFR recording with correct syntax
Can interpret thread states (RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING) in a thread dump excerpt and identify a deadlock
Can explain the difference between shallow size and retained size in a heap dump analysis
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a developer who has never profiled before: what is a flame graph, how do you read it, and what action do you take when you find a wide bar you didn't expect?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a class ProfileTarget that simulates a CPU hotspot to demonstrate profiling targets:

  1. Write a method int countWords(String text) that splits on spaces and returns the count. Use String.split(" +").
  2. Write a method String buildReport(int n) that loops n times, calling countWords with a fixed string, and builds a result string with +=.
  3. In main: call buildReport(10_000) three times (warmup), then time a fourth call and print the elapsed milliseconds.
  4. Add a comment above buildReport explaining which two performance anti-patterns it contains.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Refactor the ProfileTarget above to fix both anti-patterns: (1) replace the += string building with a StringBuilder, and (2) compile the regex pattern once as a static field. Name the refactored class ProfileTargetFixed. Re-time the same buildReport(10_000) call. Print both the time and a message confirming which pattern was fixed. Confirm word count is still correct by printing countWords("hello world java") = 3.

questions.questionHtml: In a flame graph, what does a wide horizontal bar near the top of the flame indicate?
options: A method that is rarely called
A method that consumes a large proportion of CPU time — a hotspot
A method that causes memory allocation
questions.correctAnswer: A method that consumes a large proportion of CPU time — a hotspot
questions.explanationHtml: Width in a flame graph represents the fraction of time that stack frame was present in the CPU sample. Wide = expensive. The top of the flame is where the CPU is actively running — wide bars near the top are the methods consuming the most time and are the primary targets for optimisation.

questions.questionHtml: A thread dump shows all application threads in BLOCKED state waiting for the same lock. What has likely happened?
options: The application is performing a long GC pause
A thread holding the lock is running slowly or is itself stuck — thread pool exhaustion or a lock bottleneck
The JVM is running out of heap space
The application is idle and waiting for requests
questions.correctAnswer: A thread holding the lock is running slowly or is itself stuck — thread pool exhaustion or a lock bottleneck
questions.explanationHtml: When many threads are BLOCKED on one lock, the thread holding that lock is a bottleneck. Check what the holder is doing — it may be in a slow I/O operation, a long computation, or itself BLOCKED or WAITING, creating a chain of waits. This is a classic lock contention signature — consider reducing lock scope or using concurrent data structures.

questions.questionHtml: Java Flight Recorder (JFR) has significant overhead and should only be used during development, not in production.
questions.explanationHtml: JFR is designed for production use with under 1% overhead. It uses a ring buffer and asynchronous sampling to minimise impact. Keeping it running continuously means you already have profiling data when an incident occurs — rather than having to reproduce the problem. This is why it was made free and built into the JDK (Java 11+).
